questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: The most derived override wins
questions.learningObjective: trace a three-level chain and find the override that a base-typed reference reaches

options.text: C, because the most derived override in the chain is the one that runs.
A, because the reference was declared with the type A.
options.misconception: believes the declared reference type picks the method body

options.text: B, because the reference is an A and the nearest override is one step up.
options.misconception: believes the override nearest to the reference type is the one chosen

options.text: ABC, because every override in the chain contributes a line.
options.misconception: believes each override in the chain adds itself to the answer

questions.explanation: The compiler emits a virtual call and the JVM resolves it against the class of the object actually stored, which is C, and C is the most derived class in the chain, so C's body is the one that runs. The reference type is the tempting source of the answer, because that is the only type visible on the source line, but it is checked at compile time to confirm that the method is accessible and is not consulted at run time to pick a body; the intermediate override in B is never reached because C replaces it.
questions.hint: Ask which class the stored object actually is, not what the variable is declared.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A gap in the override chain
questions.learningObjective: trace dispatch when the most derived class does not override but an ancestor does

options.text: B, because B is the most derived class that supplies an override.
A, because C declares no method and so the top class is used.
options.misconception: believes a class that declares nothing falls back to the chain's top

options.text: C, because the runtime class is named in the printed result.
options.misconception: believes the runtime class name becomes the answer by default

options.text: Nothing prints, because C inherits no method of its own.
options.misconception: believes a subclass without a body inherits nothing at all

questions.explanation: Dispatch looks for the most derived override in the whole chain, so when C contributes nothing the search continues up and settles on B's body, which is the override that actually overrides A. Falling back to A is the tempting answer, because A is the class named on the reference and is the one whose method the compiler checked, but an inherited method is looked up from the object's class upward, and the first override found on that walk is B's, not A's.
questions.hint: Walk up from the runtime class and stop at the first override you meet.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A method only the superclass declares
questions.learningObjective: state that a method with no override anywhere is inherited unchanged
questions.stem: A subclass adds fields but declares no methods at all, and a caller holds a base-typed reference to it. Which statement about calling the base class's describe() method is correct?

options.text: The superclass's body runs, inherited unchanged by the subclass instance.
No body runs, because the subclass declares no method of that name.
options.misconception: believes a method is only callable when the subclass declares it

options.text: A stub body runs, because every class needs its own copy of the method.
options.misconception: believes each class must supply its own copy of an inherited method

options.text: The call is rejected at compile time because the reference type is the base.
options.misconception: believes a base-typed reference cannot call a base method

questions.explanation: A subclass inherits every accessible instance method of its superclass, so a method that the subclass never overrides is reached on the superclass's own body; the base-typed reference is satisfied because the declared type has the method, and the runtime type has no version of its own to displace it. The compile-time-rejection belief is tempting, because narrow references are the usual source of trouble in inheritance, but a base reference is the widest case available and the method being called is the base's own.
questions.hint: Inheritance means the subclass already has the method unless it replaces it.

[P], because code inside a superclass body always runs its own version.
options.misconception: believes a method body is pinned to the class that wrote it

options.text: [Q][P], because both helpers run and both results are printed.
options.misconception: believes calling the superclass helper also runs the subclass helper

options.text: [], because mark() returns nothing when called from the parent body.
options.misconception: believes the helper yields no result when reached indirectly

questions.explanation: The call to mark() inside label() has this as its receiver, and this is the Q instance, so the same virtual lookup that chose Q's label body also chooses Q's mark body, giving [Q]. The pinned-body belief is tempting, because label() was written inside P and its own body is the one that runs, but only the entry point is fixed by the call site; every method invoked without an explicit super or this qualifier is a fresh dispatch against the runtime type.
questions.hint: Decide the receiver of the inner call, not the class that wrote the outer body.

questions.topic: A final method blocks the override
questions.learningObjective: state that a final method cannot be overridden and identify the compile error it causes

options.text: It fails to compile because a final method cannot be overridden.
It compiles and prints R, because the final version wins at run time.
options.misconception: believes a final override is accepted and settled at run time

options.text: It compiles and prints S, because the subclass declaration replaces the parent.
options.misconception: believes a same-signature method always replaces the parent one

options.text: It compiles and prints RS, because both tag bodies contribute their text.
options.misconception: believes an override is added to the inherited behaviour

questions.explanation: The final keyword closes the method to overriding at the language level, so the subclass declaration is rejected during compilation and the program never runs; the compiler's message names the overridden method as final. Expecting the parent's body to win at run time is the tempting reading, because dynamic dispatch then does favour the parent's final version, but final does not work by winning a race, it works by making the subclass declaration illegal in the first place.
questions.hint: Final is a compile-time restriction, not a run-time contest.

questions.topic: An override that delegates upward
questions.learningObjective: trace a counter that both adds its own contribution and the superclass contribution

options.text: 11, because the super call contributes 1 and the override adds 10.
10, because the super call's value is discarded by the addition.
options.misconception: believes a super call is made only for its side effects

options.text: 1, because the base-typed reference selects the base class's body.
options.misconception: believes the reference type overrides the runtime class here

options.text: 0, because the super call resets the counter before the addition runs.
options.misconception: believes a super call zeroes the accumulator for its caller

questions.explanation: The call is dispatched to C2's body, and that body evaluates super.total() as a direct non-virtual call to C1's version, which returns 1, then adds 10 to produce 11. Expecting the parent's value to be discarded is the tempting reading, because super is often pictured as a bare delegation, but here the returned number is the entire left-hand operand of the addition, so both contributions reach the result and the override is a sum rather than a replacement.
questions.hint: Work out what the super call returns before the addition happens.

questions.topic: Calling through a null base reference
questions.learningObjective: predict the failure of an instance call on a base-typed reference holding null

options.text: NullPointerException, because there is no object to dispatch on.
A, because a null reference still names the declared base type.
options.misconception: believes null carries the declared type for dispatch purposes

options.text: B, because the most derived override is selected before the value is read.
options.misconception: believes override selection happens before the reference is read

options.text: 0, because a null reference falls back to the default return value.
options.misconception: believes a null receiver yields the type's default result

questions.explanation: Dispatch needs a real receiver: the call first has to read the value out of ref, and since that value is null there is no object whose class could be consulted, so a NullPointerException is raised before any body is chosen. Believing the declared type still names a body is the tempting step, because the compiler accepted the call using the declared type alone, but that check is purely about accessibility and the run-time lookup has nothing to work with when the reference is null.
questions.hint: The runtime lookup happens after the receiver value is read.

hi, because the variable is declared with the base type D.
options.misconception: believes the base type wins once the object is stored

options.text: hi, because an anonymous body is only visible inside its own block.
options.misconception: believes an anonymous override is scoped to the block that declares it

options.text: Nothing prints, because D cannot be instantiated anonymously.
options.misconception: believes a class cannot be extended at a declaration site

questions.explanation: An anonymous class expression still creates a real class, and that generated class overrides greet, so it is the runtime type of the stored object and its body is the one chosen. The declared-type belief is the tempting one, because D is the only type written on the variable line and the anonymous block looks like a local flourish, but storing the object in a base-typed variable narrows the static view without changing what the object is, and the object is an anonymous subclass of D.
questions.hint: The expression on the right of new creates a class, not just an object.

two, because the child's method has the same name and a wider access.
options.misconception: believes a same-signature public method always overrides a parent one

options.text: two, because the child is a subclass and subclasses inherit downwards.
options.misconception: believes inheritance flows from the subclass back into the parent

options.text: onetwo, because both bodies run and their texts are concatenated.
options.misconception: believes a same-signature pair runs both bodies in turn

questions.explanation: A method with no access modifier belongs to its own package and is not inherited by a subclass in a different package, so Child2's public tag() is a new method rather than an override, and the inherited lookup through a Base2 reference stops at Base2's own package-private body. Widening the access modifier is the tempting belief, because public really is wider than package-private, but the override relation is decided by inheritance first, and nothing was inherited for the child's declaration to override.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A total summed along an override chain
questions.learningObjective: compute the value of an override that accumulates every ancestor's contribution
questions.stem: Three classes form a chain in which each override adds its own number to whatever the parent returns: class N1 has int score() returning 1, class N2 extends N1 returning super.score() + 2, and class N3 extends N2 returning super.score() + 4. A call to score() is made through a reference declared as N1 that holds a new N3(). What integer is produced? Respond with the integer only.
questions.explanation: The call reaches N3's body, which asks N2 for its value, which in turn asks N1 and adds its own 2, so the total is 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 once all three bodies have contributed. Reporting 4 is the tempting answer, because that is the number the most derived body adds by itself, but each super call returns the fully accumulated sum of everything below it rather than a bare constant, so the chain's contributions pile up instead of replacing one another.
questions.hint: Each super call returns everything accumulated so far, not just its own class's part.

options.text: It fails to compile because the field cannot be read before super runs.
It compiles and prints P1:4, because the field initializer runs first.
options.misconception: believes instance initializers run before the super constructor

options.text: It compiles and prints P1:0, because the field still holds its default.
options.misconception: believes a readable field would still hold its default value

options.text: It fails to compile because a super call must be the first line.
options.misconception: believes a super call is illegal anywhere but the first statement

questions.explanation: When the super constructor is invoked the subclass part of the object does not exist yet, so its instance field may not be named in the argument list, and the compiler reports that the field cannot be referenced before the supertype constructor has been called. The first-line belief is the tempting one, because the usual classroom picture of a super call is a mandatory opening statement, but a plain statement may precede it and this failure has nothing to do with position: it is the name width in the argument list that is forbidden.
questions.hint: Check what the argument expression names, not where the statement sits.

questions.topic: What may surround an explicit constructor call
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the statements allowed before a super or this call from the expressions forbidden inside it
questions.stem: A subclass constructor begins with a plain statement and only then calls its parent. Which statement about that arrangement is correct?

options.text: Legal, as long as the call's arguments avoid this object's fields.
Illegal, because a super call must be the first statement of a body.
options.misconception: believes a super call must always open the constructor body

options.text: Legal, and the arguments may freely read the subclass's own fields.
options.misconception: believes the argument list may read instance fields freely

options.text: Illegal, because a constructor may contain at most one statement.
options.misconception: believes a constructor body is limited to a single statement

questions.explanation: A super invocation does not have to open the constructor body, so a print or an assignment placed before it compiles and runs first, which is exactly why the superclass's own output appears after it; the restriction that does apply is on the arguments, which may not name the subclass's instance fields or use this, because the subclass half of the object does not exist yet. The mandatory-first-line belief is the tempting and extremely widespread one, but the real rule is narrower: position is free, self-reference is not.
questions.hint: Separate where the call may sit from what its arguments may name.

questions.topic: Delegating to another constructor of the same class
questions.learningObjective: trace an instance initialiser across a this delegation to a sibling constructor

options.text: W1:9, then W2(9), then W2 tag=1, because the field initializes once.
W2 tag=1, then W1:9, then W2(9), because the caller runs first.
options.misconception: believes the delegating constructor's body runs before the delegate

options.text: W1:9, then W2(9), then W2 tag=0, because the field never initializes.
options.misconception: believes a this delegation skips the instance initializer

options.text: W1:9, W2(9), W2 tag=1 twice, because each constructor initializes fields.
options.misconception: believes both constructors run the instance initializer block

questions.explanation: The call to this(9) transfers control to the sibling constructor, which calls super(9) so the parent prints W1:9, then prints W2(9), and only when that returns does the original constructor resume and print W2 tag=1; the field initializer tag = 1 is compiled into the one constructor that does not delegate, so it runs exactly once. A tag of 0 is the tempting result, because the delegating constructor's own body executes after the delegate finishes, but the initializer was already inserted into the delegate right after its super call, so the field is set before either body reaches its print.
questions.hint: Only the constructor that skips the this call carries the initializer.

questions.topic: One parent body call per constructed object
questions.learningObjective: count how often a superclass constructor body runs across a chain and several constructions
questions.stem: A chain of three classes has a constructor body in each that prints its own name: class Y1 prints Y1, class Y2 extends Y1 prints Y2, and class Y3 extends Y2 prints Y3. The program then constructs two Y3 objects in succession. How many times does the Y1 constructor body execute? Respond with the integer only.
questions.explanation: Every constructed object runs the whole chain of constructor bodies once, so each of the two Y3 objects runs Y1's body exactly once and the total is 2; a constructor in a superclass is invoked once per object, never once per subclass level or once per subclass. Six is the tempting count, because three constructor bodies times two objects gives six print lines in total, but that total is spread evenly as two of each name, and the question asks only about the topmost body.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: One superclass alongside several capabilities
questions.learningObjective: explain why a class that needs both a base and capabilities reaches for several interfaces
questions.stem: A report class must keep extending its existing base class for shared file handling and must also be printable, closeable, and loggable. Which arrangement is available in Java?

options.text: One extends clause for the base and one implements clause listing three interfaces.
Four extends clauses, one for the base and one for each capability.
options.misconception: believes Java allows one superclass plus several superclasses

options.text: One extends clause for the base, with the capabilities as abstract methods of it.
options.misconception: believes extra capabilities can be added to an existing base class

options.text: Only the base may be extended, and the capabilities must be static helpers.
options.misconception: believes a subclass cannot add capabilities at all

questions.explanation: Java permits exactly one superclass per class but an open-ended implements list, which is precisely the asymmetry that lets this report keep its inherited file handling and still be printable, closeable, and loggable. Stacking extends clauses is the tempting arrangement, because superclass and interface both express a type's obligations and read similarly in a class header, but only one class can be inherited, and a capability that is not inherited state belongs in an interface instead.
questions.hint: Count how many classes a single class may inherit directly.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A protected helper points to an abstract class
questions.learningObjective: choose an abstract class when a helper must be reachable only from within one hierarchy
questions.stem: A document hierarchy needs a shared helper that subclasses may call but no code outside the hierarchy may use. Which declaration can offer that?

options.text: An abstract class declaring the helper with the protected modifier.
An interface declaring the helper with the protected modifier.
options.misconception: believes an interface method may be declared protected

options.text: An interface declaring the helper as public so subclasses can reach it.
options.misconception: believes a public interface method excludes outside callers

options.text: A concrete class declaring the helper as private with a public wrapper.
options.misconception: believes a private helper plus a public wrapper is equivalent

questions.explanation: The access requirement is the deciding constraint: a helper that subclasses in one hierarchy may call but unrelated code may not needs protected, and protected is a member modifier a class can use while an interface method may only be public or private. Making it public on an interface is the tempting route, because public certainly lets subclasses reach it, but it also makes it public to every caller everywhere, which is exactly the access the design is trying to prevent.
questions.hint: Check which access modifiers an interface member is allowed to use.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A shared method reading a base-declared field
questions.learningObjective: trace a concrete base method that reads a field the base itself declares

options.text: 10, because the base's concrete method runs and reads its own field.
0, because the base's concrete method has no subclass body to run.
options.misconception: believes a concrete base method is skipped for a subclass

options.text: 5, because bill() returns the field and ignores the abstract rate.
options.misconception: believes the shared method skips the varying step entirely

options.text: Nothing prints, because an abstract class cannot declare a field.
options.misconception: believes an abstract class may not declare instance fields

questions.explanation: The reference is typed as Meter, so the concrete bill() that Meter declares is the body reached, and inside that body the field units and the call to rate() are both resolved against the Flat object, giving 5 * 2 = 10. Expecting no body to run is the tempting thought, because bill() appears inside an abstract class, but abstract applies to the whole class not to each of its methods, and a concrete method in an abstract class is a perfectly normal shared implementation.
questions.hint: Abstract marks the class, not every method inside it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A behaviour-free marker points to an interface
questions.learningObjective: choose an empty interface when a type only needs to be tagged for later use
questions.stem: A test framework needs to recognise which classes should be collected for a report, and it will decide what to do with them later by casting. Which declaration carries that tag?

options.text: An interface with no methods, which the chosen classes implement.
An abstract class with no methods, which the chosen classes extend.
options.misconception: believes a behaviour-free tag needs an abstract class

options.text: A concrete class with no fields, which the chosen classes extend.
options.misconception: believes an empty concrete class is a suitable tag

options.text: An interface with one method the chosen classes already have by some other name.
options.misconception: believes a marker must require a method to work

questions.explanation: What the framework needs is only a type it can test for and cast to, and an interface with an empty body supplies exactly that without forcing the tagged classes into one inheritance tree, which matters because they are otherwise unrelated. An abstract class is the tempting answer, because abstract is the keyword people reach for when a base has nothing to do, but abstract still means a superclass, so adopting the tag would cost each class its own freedom to extend something else.
questions.hint: Ask what the framework does with the tag: test for it, or inherit from it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Implementation work fanned out by an abstract class
questions.learningObjective: count the concrete bodies an abstract class requires across its subclasses
questions.stem: An abstract base declares three abstract methods, and four subclasses each supply a concrete body for all three of them. Across all four subclasses together, how many concrete method bodies must be written for those three methods? Respond with the integer only.
questions.explanation: An abstract method is a promise rather than a body, so each of the four subclasses writes its own three implementations and the total is 4 * 3 = 12 concrete bodies across the design. Three is the tempting count, because the base declares three methods and the shape looks like a single shared contract, but the declarations are not implementations, and nothing in the language lets four subclasses share one body unless the base supplies a concrete default they may inherit.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of declared abstract methods by the number of subclasses.

questions.topic: Declaring an abstract base and its abstract step
questions.learningObjective: complete an abstract class declaration with a constructor and an abstract method

options.text: abstract class Ticket
interface Ticket
options.misconception: believes an interface may hold the abstract fee method here

options.text: class Ticket
options.misconception: believes a plain class may declare an abstract method

options.text: abstract class Standard
options.misconception: believes the header must name the subclass instead

questions.explanation: The header must be abstract class Ticket, because a class is what Standard extends and because a class is the construct that may declare an abstract method awaiting a subclass body. Naming the subclass is the tempting slip, since Standard is the concrete class in the file, but a subclass cannot extend itself and the abstract declaration has to sit on the type being extended.
questions.hint: Check which name the extends clause refers to.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Keeping a base from being instantiated
questions.learningObjective: compare how an abstract class and a concrete class prevent direct construction
questions.stem: A base type exists only to be extended, and no code may build it directly. Which arrangement keeps that guarantee with the least code?

options.text: Declare the base abstract, because abstractness alone blocks direct construction.
Declare the base concrete and give it a constructor with a private modifier.
options.misconception: believes an abstract class needs a private constructor as well

options.text: Declare the base abstract and also give it a private constructor.
options.misconception: believes abstractness does not block direct construction

options.text: Declare the base abstract and add a runtime guard that throws in its body.
options.misconception: believes an abstract constructor must throw to be safe

questions.explanation: A type marked abstract cannot be the target of a new expression at all, so declaring the base abstract already blocks direct construction and needs nothing else; a private constructor is the technique for a base that must remain concrete, which is the case a design reaches only when the class has no abstract steps to offer. Adding a private constructor to an abstract class is the tempting belt-and-braces move, but it is redundant, and the throw-in-the-body version would be dead code because no call can ever get that far.
questions.hint: Ask whether the language already forbids new on this type.
